answers.answer: Replication copies data changes between servers; each maintained copy is a replica. Replication keeps the same data on several servers, whereas sharding divides data into different groups; each group can itself have replicas. Copies can serve reads and take over after a failure, but read routing and safe takeover require separate work, lag can produce old reads, and more copies do not automatically increase write capacity. Start a new replica with a snapshot, a copy at a known point, then send the source change log: records of later changes. Apply those changes by updating the replica data, preserving required source order; an older dependent change applied late can restore an outdated value. The snapshot and starting log position must match so changes are neither missed nor applied incorrectly. The replica tracks progress to resume after a disconnect. Receiving records is distinct from updating query-visible data, so receipt alone does not make a read fresh. The lesson does not specify an implementation for coordinating the snapshot/log boundary.

evidence.quote: Copies data changes between servers. Each maintained copy is a replica.
Read routing and a safe takeover process are separate design work; a second copy does not configure either automatically.
Adding read replicas can increase read capacity. It does not automatically increase the number of writes the system can handle.
The initial copy and starting log position must agree. Otherwise the handoff can miss changes or apply them incorrectly. Each replication implementation coordinates that boundary.

Records later changes on the source. The replica receives these records and applies them while preserving the required source order. Applying an older change after a newer dependent change could restore an out-of-date value.
The replica updated its data so queries can see the change.

answers.answer: Asynchronous replication permits the writing server to acknowledge success before a replica confirms the change. An acknowledgement says the configured success condition was met, not that another server or every copy has the write. A write can succeed on the primary, be acknowledged to the application, then be lost with the primary before reaching a replica; promoting that replica cannot preserve the missing change. Avoiding the replica wait reduces write waiting but permits stale reads and loss of recent acknowledged writes at failover. Synchronous replication waits for required replica confirmations before success. Specify the required set or count and the confirmation stage: received may mean memory only, stored durably means storage that survives restart, and applied means queries can see the updated data. Waiting for durable replicas protects against losing the writing server but adds delay and dependence on their availability. If an unavailable replica leaves too few required confirmations, writes can stall. Success need not involve every replica, and receipt or durable storage need not imply application, so synchronous success does not guarantee all replica reads are current. It protects against specified failures, not loss of every copy or accidental logical changes. The lesson supplies no exact latency, timeout, or replica-count configuration.

evidence.quote: The writing server can acknowledge success before a replica confirms the change. Acknowledgement means the configured success condition was met, not that every copy has the data.
If the writing server fails permanently before sending a confirmed change, a replacement replica will not have that change.
A write waits for confirmation from the required replicas before reporting success. What that confirmation means matters.
The replica has the change, possibly only in memory.
The replica saved it to storage that can survive a restart.
The replica updated its data so queries can see the change.
Waiting for durable copies protects against losing the writing server. It adds delay, and writes can stall if too few required replicas respond.
Choose the required replica set or count and acknowledgement stage. This protects against specified failures, not loss of every copy or accidental logical changes.

answers.answer: Replication lag means a replica is behind in receiving or applying source changes. A successful write can precede its application on the replica selected for a later read, so that read returns the older value. Read-after-write behavior here means read-your-writes: later reads include your completed change or newer state. Reading from the still-authoritative primary holding the write avoids waiting for replica application but concentrates load and requires correct authority after failover. Waiting for evidence that a selected replica applied this particular write allows a fresh replica read, but adds delay and can fail; fixed sleeps or low average lag are insufficient proof. Accepting stale reads suits delay-tolerant work and permits using replicas without waiting for that write, but does not provide read-your-writes. No routing choice recovers a write already lost at failover. A leader accepts writes: a single leader accepts them for a dataset and orders them in one place, while followers copy changes; replacing it requires failover. Multiple leaders accept writes and exchange changes, potentially allowing nearby writes; independent updates of the same item need a conflict rule, and choosing the latest timestamp can discard a valid edit. In a leaderless arrangement, a coordinating server sends requests to the replicas holding the data, waits for the configured number of replies, and differences must be repaired; concurrent versions still need reconciliation. More write-accepting servers do not guarantee conflict-free updates or one current value. These arrangements alone do not specify synchronous versus asynchronous replication. Exact routing, reconciliation algorithms and latency figures are not supplied.

evidence.quote: A replica is behind the source in receiving or applying changes. State which stage a lag measurement describes; data received but not applied is not yet visible to reads.
Later reads include your own completed change or newer state. Read from the authoritative primary holding the write, or wait for evidence that the selected replica applied that specific change.
Primary reads concentrate load and require correct authority after failover. Waiting for a replica adds delay and can fail. Routing alone cannot recover a write already lost during failover.
One server accepts writes for a set of data. Followers copy its changes. This gives writes one place to be ordered, but replacing that leader requires a failover process.

Several servers accept writes and exchange changes. This can let users write to a nearby server. If two leaders change the same item independently, the system needs a conflict rule. Choosing the latest timestamp can discard another valid edit.

Requests can go through any coordinating server, which sends them to the replicas holding the data. The system waits for a configured number of replies and repairs differences between copies. Concurrent versions still need reconciliation; no topology name guarantees one current value or conflict-free updates.

answers.answer: Failover transfers a failed server’s responsibilities to another server. In a single-leader system promotion makes the selected replica the leader. Split brain means two servers both act as sole leader and can accept conflicting changes. Silence does not establish death: the old leader may have a broken network connection while still accepting writes. Select a suitable sufficiently current replica because its progress affects survival of recent writes; fence the old leader by preventing further writes, for example by shutting it down or blocking access; promote the replacement and redirect application connections to it. This supplies both a replacement and protection against competing authoritative writers. The lesson does not define a precise eligibility check or promotion protocol. Acknowledged asynchronous writes absent from the replacement can be lost. A healthy current replica can also have faithfully copied an accidental deletion, so it cannot necessarily recover earlier data. A backup preserves an earlier recoverable state; point-in-time recovery restores a backup and replays saved logs up to a chosen moment, such as just before the deletion. Retention and available logs limit how far back recovery can go. Restore tests must reconstruct usable application data and measure recovery duration. An untested backup’s mere existence, or a current replica alone, proves neither recovery time nor recoverable history; takeover and historical restoration both need testing.

evidence.quote: Moves a failed server's responsibilities to another server. In a single-leader system, the process selects a suitable replica, promotes it to leader, and redirects application connections. How current that replica is affects whether recent writes survive.
A missing response does not prove the old leader stopped. Its network connection can be broken while it still accepts writes.
Happens when two servers both act as the sole leader. They can accept conflicting changes.
Prevents the old leader from continuing to write, for example by shutting it down or blocking its access.
Replication also copies unwanted changes. If someone deletes the wrong records, replicas can apply that deletion too.
Restores a backup and replays saved change logs up to a chosen moment. That can recover the database to just before an accidental deletion.
Retention and available logs bound recoverable history. Restore tests must reconstruct usable application data and measure how long recovery takes; file existence alone proves neither.

answers.answer: Proposed policy: first establish how much acknowledged-write loss is acceptable and for which failures, how stale reporting reads may be, what write delay is acceptable, and how long recovery downtime may last. Use a single writing leader with replicas, requiring synchronous durable acknowledgement from a specified replica set or count chosen against those failure and latency targets. This minimizes some loss windows if the writer is lost, at the cost of commit delay and stalled writes if too few required replicas respond. Route delay-tolerant reports to replicas within the agreed freshness requirement; use the authoritative primary holding the write or evidence of application of the specific write for freshness-sensitive reads. Exercise takeover by selecting a suitable current replica, fencing the former leader, promoting the replacement and updating routing. Keep backups and retained logs for historical recovery, and test restoration to usable application data within the required time and retention targets. Monitor replication progress, the receive/apply stage of lag, health, write waits and recovery measurements; account for storage, network and operating costs. The exact replica count, acceptable lag, retention duration, recovery target and implementation cannot be determined from the supplied requirements. Replication alone specifies none of these guarantees: asynchronous acknowledgement may precede another copy, synchronous protection covers specified failures rather than every loss, unwanted deletions can replicate, and operations needing unreachable copies must wait or fail during a network split. Therefore neither zero loss nor uninterrupted writes follows from the word replication.

evidence.quote: Choose acceptable acknowledged-write loss, read freshness, write latency and recovery time before choosing replica settings.

Delay-tolerant reads can use replicas. Freshness-sensitive reads need suitable routing or progress checks. Waiting for durable replica acknowledgements narrows some loss windows but adds commit delay and dependence on those replicas.
Copies consume storage, network and operating work. Monitor replication progress, lag, health and write waits; exercise failover and historical restore against the required recovery targets.
During a network split, operations that need agreement with unreachable copies must wait or fail. Independent operation instead needs explicit handling of old reads and conflicting writes.
Choose the required replica set or count and acknowledgement stage. This protects against specified failures, not loss of every copy or accidental logical changes.
Replication helps keep service running after a server failure. Backups and retained logs help recover earlier data.
